problem: Traditional planners for unknown indoor environments (e.g. DYNUS) rely on local heuristics and goal projection, so they enter dead ends such as small rooms and must backtrack, producing inefficient paths.
motivation: Robots in cluttered unknown buildings (delivery, search-and-rescue) have no prior map, and greedy goal-directed exploration wastes travel. VLMs can recognize structure such as rooms, corridors and dead ends from floor-plan-like images, so they may supply the missing global reasoning on top of a safe trajectory planner.
key_idea: Render the partial 3D occupancy grid as an annotated 2D map image, and have a zero-shot VLM score frontier-based candidate subgoals, aggregating samples by median belief, to steer a trajectory planner (DYNUS) away from dead ends.
insight: The VLM works better as a scorer over pre-generated candidates than as a subgoal generator or policy, and an image map worked better than a string map. GPT-4.1's rationales show it identifies rooms, hallways and dead ends and trades off progress against unknown space. The main bottleneck is map quality: when the map is mostly unknown or erroneous, performance degrades. Only one end-to-end comparison (DYNUS vs DYNUS+VLM) is reported, with no ablations of the median aggregation, n, or map format beyond a remark.
method: Map representation: project the online 3D voxel/occupancy map to a 2D grid with free/unknown/occupied cells, marking a cell free only if it has z-clearance and is reachable; overlay robot, goal and candidates, and pass it as an image (better than a string). It is down-sampled to 60x60 cells covering 24x24 m.

Candidate subgoal generation: mark free cells adjacent to unknown cells (8-neighborhood) as frontiers, cluster them, take the cell nearest each cluster centroid, and deduplicate route-equivalent candidates. The terminal goal or its projection is added if reachable.

VLM scoring: GPT-4.1 receives the map and a detailed developer prompt (wall tracing, enclosure check, corridor/room classification, progress toward goal, risk). It assigns each candidate a belief that it is best, summing to 1, plus a short rationale.

Robust aggregation: sample n=3 responses per query, take the per-candidate median belief and normalize it, compute the median absolute deviation as an uncertainty measure, and choose the highest-belief candidate.
Integration with DYNUS: the VLM only picks the high-level subgoal, and the optimization-based DYNUS planner does trajectory generation with safety guarantees.
grid-world tool: a 2D simulator built to study LLM/VLM navigation, visualizing median belief and MAD per candidate.

setting.backbone: GPT-4.1 (gpt-4.1-2025-04-14, frozen) as high-level scorer; DYNUS as trajectory planner
setting.observation: 3D occupancy grid built online (no RGB), projected to 2D map image with robot, goal and candidates
setting.action_space: high-level subgoals chosen from frontier candidates, executed by DYNUS trajectory planner (continuous, max 1.0 m/s)
setting.privileged: none (goal position given as the task target)

numbers.eval_set_note: 15 trials in one Gazebo office environment
numbers.backbone: GPT-4.1 (gpt-4.1-2025-04-14), n=3, image map 60x60 cells / 24x24 m
numbers.extra: max speed/acc/jerk 1.0 m/s, 3.0 m/s^2, 4.0 m/s^3; baseline DYNUS 42.0 ± 3.2 m
numbers.evidence: Table 1: Average path length (± std) over 15 runs in a Gazebo office environment: DYNUS + GPT-4.1 (Ours) 37.9 ± 3.8

numbers_note: Only one experiment (single custom Gazebo office scenario); no standard benchmark results.
results: In a Gazebo office over 15 runs, adding the VLM planner cut average path length from 42.0 ± 3.2 m (DYNUS alone) to 37.9 ± 3.8 m, about 10% shorter. Qualitatively it stays in hallways and avoids small rooms when far from the goal.
limitations: Evaluation is a single simulated office environment with 15 trials, with no real robot and no ablations.
Performance degrades with maps dominated by unknown space or containing errors, and poorly placed candidate subgoals cause some inefficient paths.
